title: SQL CROSS JOIN
learningObjectives: Explain the Cartesian-product behaviour of CROSS JOIN.
Write explicit CROSS JOIN queries between two input tables.
Calculate the expected row count from the sizes of both inputs.
Filter and calculate values across generated combinations.
Recognize the performance risks of unexpectedly large Cartesian products.

understand.concept: CROSS JOIN combines every row from the first table with every row from the second table. If the inputs contain m and n rows, the result contains m × n rows. It does not require a matching-key condition.
understand.whyItMatters: Cartesian products are useful for generating combinations such as products by regions, dates by shifts, or students by available sessions. They can also create unexpectedly large results if used without care.
understand.analogy: Imagine pairing every item in one short list with every option in another list.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not show how quickly row counts grow when both lists become large or how filters and duplicate input rows affect the result.

examples.title: Create the two independent input tables
examples.explanation: The sample contains two products and three shipping regions.

examples.title: Generate every product and region combination
examples.expectedOutput: Notebook | North; Notebook | South; Notebook | East; Desk Lamp | North; Desk Lamp | South; Desk Lamp | East
examples.explanation: A CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product: two product rows multiplied by three region rows gives six combinations.

examples.title: Calculate a regional price for each combination
examples.expectedOutput: Notebook | North | 70; Notebook | South | 75; Notebook | East | 65; Desk Lamp | North | 220; Desk Lamp | South | 225; Desk Lamp | East | 215
examples.explanation: The result can be used to create a product-by-region pricing matrix.

examples.title: Filter combinations after the Cartesian product
examples.expectedOutput: Notebook | North; Notebook | East; Desk Lamp | North; Desk Lamp | East
examples.explanation: The WHERE condition reduces the generated combinations to regions whose fee is at most 20.

examples.title: Count combinations for each product
examples.explanation: Each product is paired with every region, so each product has three combinations.

practise.guidedTask: Run the sample setup and predict the row count before running the CROSS JOIN. Add a WHERE condition to keep only one region, then compare the new count.
practise.independentTask: Create a table of at least four courses and another table of three time slots. Generate all course-slot combinations, calculate a booking fee, filter selected time slots, and explain the expected row count before execution.
hints: Multiply the row counts to predict the Cartesian result size.
CROSS JOIN does not use ON.
Use aliases to make column references clear.
Use WHERE to reduce combinations after generation.
Use ORDER BY when the display order matters.

options: Every combination of rows from both inputs
All rows from the left input only
questions.answer: Every combination of rows from both inputs
questions.explanation: A Cartesian product pairs each left row with each right row.

questions.prompt: If the first table has 4 rows and the second has 3, how many rows are produced?
questions.explanation: The Cartesian product has 4 × 3 = 12 row pairs.

questions.prompt: Does a CROSS JOIN require an ON condition?
options: Only when both tables have primary keys
questions.explanation: CROSS JOIN generates all combinations and does not use a matching predicate.

questions.prompt: Which clause can reduce the combinations returned?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters the generated row combinations.

questions.prompt: What is a major risk of an unintended CROSS JOIN?
options: Conversion of all values to NULL
questions.explanation: The number of result rows is the product of the two input row counts.
